title: The fakir in Dwarkamai
hookLine: a fakir moves into a crumbling mosque and gives it a name from Krishna's city
tomorrow: a weaver lies down on the dark river steps. why?

lines: A ROOM WITH A NEW NAME.
A FIRE IN AN OLD MOSQUE.
cards: A new room in a new city, nothing on the walls yet. Some people make a place home by giving it a name. In the village of Shirdi, a fakir, a wandering holy man, does that with a run-down old mosque.
He moves in. He keeps a fire burning and hands its ash to whoever comes. And he calls the mosque Dwarkamai, a name that echoes Dwarka, Krishna's city.
The visitors keep asking the same thing: is this man Hindu, or Muslim?

teach.b: This is Sai Baba of Shirdi, as the Shri Sai Satcharitra remembers him, a book written in Marathi by a devotee. And the book admits the puzzle.
People couldn't settle whether he was Hindu or Muslim, and he didn't settle it for them. On his lips, the book says, was Allah Malik: God is the master.
He handed out the ash of his fire, called udi, and the book tells story after story of people who carried it home. Then the festival.
A fair for Ram Navami, Ram's birthday, grew up at Shirdi, and on that same day Muslim devotees carried a sandalwood procession for a saint. Side by side, each kept by its own people.
So how could a Hindu bow to a fakir in a mosque? Through a very Hindu practice: darshan, going to see a holy one, and being seen. Hindus seek darshan wherever holiness shows.
In Hindu devotion, a guru who lives close to God is often honored as a doorway to God.
That's why Hindu devotees waved arati lamps before him, and why many homes still keep his picture near Ganesha and Krishna.

teach.h: DARSHAN: SEE THE HOLY, BE SEEN.
teach.b: Some Hindus honor him as a guru, some as God among people. Some Muslims remember him as a Sufi fakir. Nobody forced a vote.
And when someone asks why your grandmother's shelf holds a fakir, that's the answer: she isn't switching sides.
She's going where she sees holiness.

how: Hindu devotees take darshan of Sai Baba of Shirdi, honoring him as a guru or as divine, wave arati before his image and keep his udi (sacred ash); some Muslims remember him as a Sufi fakir. The Shri Sai Satcharitra, written in Marathi by a devotee, is a central account of his life.

o: village holy men who changed their religion more than once
holy people both Hindus and Muslims remember as their own
festivals that two faiths celebrate together as one

p: his name for the old mosque
the ash of his fire, carried home
seeing a holy one, and being seen

s: the Satcharitra says Sai Baba declared himself a Hindu
it says people couldn't settle it, and he didn't settle it for them.
at Shirdi, Ram Navami and a sandal procession fell on the same day
two observances, one day, each kept by its own people.
a Hindu who honors Sai Baba has left Hinduism
darshan follows holiness: Hindus honor a holy one without switching sides.

games.q: your aunt comes back from a Sai Baba temple and dabs a little udi on your forehead. a friend asks: wait, does your family worship a Muslim saint? what fits what you learned?
o: she went for darshan: Hindus honor holiness where they see it, and nobody switched sides.
yes, so your family must have quietly become Muslim.
no, udi is just a lucky charm with no meaning at all.
games.why: Darshan follows holiness. Hindus waved arati before Sai Baba; Muslims remembered him as a fakir; the Satcharitra never forced a vote.

practice: This is darshan at home. If you have a lamp, a candle, or a picture you hold sacred, sit before it and look softly, as if you're being looked at in return. If you like, circle the light once, slowly, the way families do at arati.
If you don't pray, rest your eyes on the brightest spot in the room and let the breath come and go.

wordCard.voice: Hindu-Muslim shared saints. Here, Sai Baba of Shirdi: honored by Hindus through darshan, remembered by Muslims as a fakir, two observances kept side by side.

orig.note: Dwarkamai, Sai Baba's name for the old mosque at Shirdi, echoing Dwarka, Krishna's city.

carryVoice: For the road: darshan follows holiness, not labels. A fakir by his fire in an old mosque showed it. The shared saints, complete.

sources.ref: Shri Sai Satcharitra: Sai Baba's life in the old mosque he called Dwarkamai, the dhuni and its ash (udi), 'Allah Malik', the uncertainty over whether he was Hindu or Muslim, and the Ram Navami fair held on the same day as the sandal procession (chapter numbers to confirm)
